prompt: Who directs the means of communication to be provided and the priorities?
options: The signal officer
The staff users
The higher headquarters' signal unit
The commander
explanation: After listing the sources of requirements, the handout states that the commander directs the means to be provided and the priorities.

prompt: Why does the handout list staff guidance as a source of voice requirements?
options: Staff officers are the users
Staff officers approve the signal budget
Staff officers write the CEOI
Staff officers operate the radios
explanation: Staff guidance is a source of requirements because staff officers are the users of signal support.

prompt: By what other name is the signal estimate known, and when is it revised?
options: The signal plan; it is fixed once published
The CEOI; it is revised every 24 hours
The C4S annex; it is revised only after the operation has ended
The C4S estimate; it is revised as the situation changes
explanation: The signal estimate examines all factors that may affect signal support. It is also called the C4S estimate and is revised as the situation changes.

prompt: According to section 2.4, when is a voice requirement worth stating?
options: When it supports a decision or an action
When equipment is available to support it
When a subordinate unit requests a net
When commercial means can meet it
explanation: A requirement is worth stating only if it supports a decision or an action. The planner asks which information requirement or task needs the link and what happens if it fails.

prompt: A planner records that the forward command post must talk while on the move. Which requirement field holds this?
options: Reach
Mobility
Availability
Quality
explanation: Mobility records whether a station is fixed, on the halt or on the move. Reach covers distance and terrain, availability the hours and restoration time.

prompt: Which requirement field asks whether intelligible voice is enough or a telephone-quality call is needed?
options: Security
Precedence
Net or service
Quality
explanation: The quality field asks whether intelligible voice is enough or a telephone-quality call is needed.

prompt: What does the handout say about telephone service on the fixed system?
options: The Army is shifting to IP telephony on PANET
Telephones are limited to coalition operations
IP telephony replaces all tactical radio nets
Telephones are a special purpose means only
explanation: In the fixed category the voice use is the telephone, and the Army is shifting to IP telephony on PANET.

prompt: What does DBTOCS do?
options: It links the Army to commercial satellite services
It provides radio over IP to rifle squads
It extends fixed communications to brigades
It manages spectrum assignments with the NTC
explanation: DBTOCS, the deployable brigade tactical operations center system, extends fixed communications to brigades (PAM 6-0102 0133).

prompt: Which list gives the components of the fixed system in PAM 6-00 0403?
options: Radios, repeaters, antennas and batteries
Transmission, switching, cable, terminal and support facilities
Command, administrative, fires and emergency nets
Primary, alternate, contingency and emergency means
explanation: The fixed system has transmission facilities (AFP FCS), switching, cable, terminal (telephones and computers) and support facilities (buildings, power, environmental control).

prompt: On the operational-to-tactical link, what is the secondary means under PAM 6-00 0406?
options: HF/SSB with VHF/FM or UHF/FM
AFP FCS if technically feasible
Commercial landline or mobile
Mobile communications systems
explanation: Operational to tactical: primary AFP FCS if technically feasible, secondary HF/SSB with VHF/FM or UHF/FM, and other means such as repeaters at strategic areas and commercial landline or mobile.

prompt: Why do repeaters on high ground extend VHF and UHF?
options: Repeaters turn VHF signals into HF skywave
VHF and UHF need line of sight between stations, and hills block it
Repeaters encrypt clear-voice radios
Repeaters on high ground cancel the effects of season and time of day on VHF
explanation: VHF and UHF depend on line of sight between stations, so hills block them and repeaters on high ground extend them.

prompt: What limitation of HF does the handout's supplementary note give?
options: It cannot reach beyond line of sight
It works only from fixed stations
Conditions vary with time of day and season, and reception can be noisy
It always needs a repeater on high ground to get past the hills between stations
explanation: HF can reach over the horizon, but conditions vary with time of day and season and reception can be noisy.

prompt: How may special purpose means be used for voice?
options: For any traffic, because commercial services are exempt from COMSEC
As the primary means for classified command traffic
Only by coalition partners in their own networks
For routine and administrative traffic and as gap fillers, with prudence and within COMSEC policy
explanation: Special purpose means carry routine and administrative traffic and act as gap fillers, used with prudence and within COMSEC policy.

prompt: Under PAM 6-0102 0311c, when does the plan provide for employing the cyber response team?
options: Whenever a radio is captured
Only after a typhoon strikes
When the vigilance net is opened
Where network attack is expected
explanation: Recovery includes changing frequencies when equipment is compromised (0311d) and employing the cyber response team where network attack is expected (0311c).

prompt: How must a disaster response radio net relate to the Army's secured operational net?
options: It must be different from and separate to it
It must be bridged to it so agencies receive orders
It must use the same encryption keys
It must replace it during the disaster
explanation: In disaster response the radio net must be different from and separate to the Army's secured operational net.

prompt: How is the disaster response net treated?
options: As confidential and limited to Army stations
As secret, with ciphertext and double talk on every single call
As unclassified and unsecured, connecting many entities
As a coalition partner's sovereign network
explanation: The disaster response net is treated as unclassified and unsecured, and it connects many entities.

prompt: Which pair does the handout name as part of electronic protection?
options: Frequency hopping and anti-jamming
Double talk and messengers
Satellite phones and cellular phones
Repeaters and commercial base radios
explanation: Electronic warfare has support, attack and protect parts, including frequency hopping and anti-jamming (PAM 6-0102 0223).

prompt: What does step 5, prepare a tentative plan (0312), contain?
options: The requirements gathered from the commander, the staff and adjacent headquarters
The chart of available equipment, personnel and funds
The final check of reconnaissance, propagation, coverage and gaps
A concept with primary, alternate, contingency and emergency plans, resource allocation, siting of centers, security, and interconnection and alternate routing
explanation: The tentative plan (0312) holds the concept with PACE plans, allocation of resources, siting of centers, security, and interconnection and alternate routing.

prompt: Which PAM 6-0102 paragraph covers developing recovery procedures?
explanation: Develop recovery procedures is step 4, paragraph 0311: how to restore service after failure.

prompt: Why are two radios on the same repeater not an alternate?
options: Two radios cannot share a repeater frequency
An alternate must always be a messenger
Repeaters are special purpose means
Each PACE level should fail differently from the one above it, and both fail with the repeater
explanation: The handout advises choosing each PACE level so it fails differently from the one above it. Two radios on the same repeater are not an alternate.

prompt: Which is one of the joint operations options the handout lists?
options: Keeping each service on a sovereign network with no integration
Treating the joint net as unclassified and unsecured
Lending equipment to another service
Using commercial cellular as the only link between services
explanation: Joint options are the vigilance net, lending equipment to another service, embedding Army radio operators in other services, or embedding their operators with our nearest TOC.

prompt: What should each net in the voice plan be given under section 4.5?
options: A call sign and one frequency, with membership decided on the day
A purpose, a net control station, a member list, primary and alternate frequencies, and a rule for who may break in
A budget line, a maintenance schedule and a spare-parts list
A commercial carrier, a phone number and a billing account
explanation: Each net needs a purpose, a net control station, a member list, a primary and alternate frequency, and a rule for who may break in.

prompt: In the voice plan, where do call signs and frequencies come from, and where do instructions for using them come from?
options: Call signs and frequencies from the CESI; how to use them from the CEOI
Both from the unit SOP
Call signs and frequencies from the CEOI; how to use them from the CESI
Both from the C4S annex
explanation: Use the CEOI for call signs and frequencies and the CESI for how to use them.

prompt: Which group of items is a personnel consideration under PAM 6-0102 0308?
options: Authorized (TE), on hand, serviceable, unserviceable, reserve pool and capability
Installation, operation and maintenance of C4 systems
Authorized (TO), actual fill-up, training status, critical shortages, committed or deployed, and reserve
Call signs, frequencies and net members
explanation: Personnel (0308) covers authorized (TO), actual fill-up, training status, critical shortages, committed or deployed, and reserve. TE items belong to equipment (0307).

prompt: What does the equipment chart under PAM 6-0102 0307 track?
options: Authorized (TO), actual fill-up, training status and critical shortages
Authorized (TE), on hand, in use or serviceable, unserviceable, reserve pool and capability of each item
Installation, operation and maintenance costs of C4 systems
Net purpose, net control station and member list
explanation: Equipment (0307) covers authorized (TE), on hand, in use or serviceable, unserviceable, reserve pool and the capability of each item.

prompt: Which task does the handout list for SMMART but not for the SMTF?
options: Visiting brigades, battalions and companies
Level 1 to 2 repairs of UHF commercial radios
Radio programming
Level 3 repairs of tactical HF radios
explanation: Both facilities repair UHF commercial radios at level 1 to 2 and program radios. Only SMMART visits brigades, battalions and companies; only the SMTF repairs tactical HF and VHF radios up to level 3.

prompt: Why do radio operators of non-signal units need refresher training?
options: Their radios change bands every year
Skills are perishable
They must replace the signal platoon
The NTC licenses each operator per operation
explanation: Skills are perishable, so radio operators of non-signal units need refresher training (PAM 6-00 0447 to 0450).

prompt: What does the handout say about commercial phones and radios?
options: They replace tactical systems in every phase
They are prohibited in all operations
They may complement tactical systems without sacrificing security
They may carry classified command traffic as long as the users encrypt it themselves
explanation: Commercial phones and radios may complement tactical systems, and facilities may be leveraged for services, without sacrificing security (PAM 6-00 0407 and 0514).
